title: SRE: Customer firewall UDP blockage retrospective and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This doc captures the incident on 2026-02-12 where a single customer VPC (tenant-382) observed intermittent control-plane reachability loss for ~45 minutes due to a customer-side firewall policy that started dropping UDP/123 (NTP) and UDP/514 (syslog) flows at scale. The control plane itself was reachable from our side, but heartbeat and metadata sync spikes led to repeated session resets and autoscaling thrash for the private control-plane proxies. Impact was partial: API requests from the customer’s private agents experienced elevated 5xx rates and latency spikes, and one internal metric ingest pipeline missed ~12 minutes of telemetry.

Why this matters:
- Private deployments rely on bidirectional lightweight control traffic (heartbeats, KV sync, health pings) often over UDP and occasionally over ephemeral source ports. Customers (or their network security teams) sometimes apply aggressive stateful rules that assume TCP-like behavior. When those rules are applied to UDP flows in a high-rate environment, intermittent drops can cascade into state desynchronization.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 2026-02-12 02:17 — First alert: increased controller resyncs observed (monitoring alert SRE-CTRL-RESYNC-1).
- 2026-02-12 02:20 — On-call pulled into #sre-oncall, began triage. Initial checks: control plane hosts healthy, no disk or CPU anomalies.
- 2026-02-12 02:27 — Customer report via support channel: "our agents intermittently fail to register". Customer provided firewall rules change log showing a scheduled update at 02:05.
- 2026-02-12 02:33 — SRE verified packet drop patterns using tcpdump on an agent host: large number of out-of-order/ICMP unreachable messages traced to customer FW appliance.
- 2026-02-12 02:40 — Temporary mitigation: increased control-plane heartbeat window (config flag: control.heartbeat.backoff_ms) to tolerate retransmits; instructed customer to roll back firewall ACLs.
- 2026-02-12 03:02 — Customer rolled back change; metrics returned to baseline by 03:12. Incident declared resolved at 03:20 after monitoring for stable 30 minutes.

Root cause analysis:
- Immediate cause: customer firewall rule update applied a stateful UDP inspection policy that began coalescing/dropping high-rate UDP flows originating from the customer's agents. The firewall treated agent heartbeats and telemetry bursts as suspicious and imposed per-flow limits.
- Contributing factors:
  - Our agent-control protocol assumes UDP for some small control messages and didn’t include robust fallback to TCP for all control-plane traffic.
  - No automated detection in the control-plane to surface sudden increases in ICMP unreachable / UDP error rates from a tenant. Alerts were tied to higher-level resync metrics which are slower to fire.
  - Runbook gap: current network runbook assumes customer-side NAT/firewall is configured permissively for ephemeral UDP but lacks explicit checklist items to validate stateful UDP inspection behavior.

Mitigations taken during incident:
- Increased heartbeat tolerance to suppress immediate autoscaling thrash.
- Confirmed customer rollback of firewall change.
- SRE added a temporary alert on UDP ICMP unreachable counts for tenant control-plane hosts.

Permanent actions and owner assignments (short-term):
- SRE: Expand control-plane telemetry to emit UDP error counters per tenant and add a fast-firing alert (owner: Jamal Thompson, ETA: 2026-02-28).
- Solutions Eng: Update onboarding checklist for Private to include explicit firewall rules template that mentions UDP stateful inspection caveats and recommended bypass for agent control ports (owner: Irene Gomez, ETA: 2026-03-05).
- Runtime: Add TCP fallback for critical control messages where ordering/size permits; prototype gating via feature flag (owner: Marcus Patel, ETA: 2026-04-15).
- Docs: Confluence page update with example iptables and ASA rules and a troubleshooting FAQ section for UDP drops (owner: Samantha Liu, ETA: 2026-03-01).

Longer-term changes (research & infra):
- Evaluate use of QUIC (TLS-over-UDP) for control plane to get reliability + congestion control while preserving lower latency. (Research owner: Applied ML infra team, ETA: Q3 2026).
- Implement synthetic agent probes from the control plane into customer VPCs that exercise UDP and TCP control flows in a low-rate fashion and report back protocol health metrics.

Runbook draft: immediate on-call steps when tenant control-plane reachability alerts occur
- 1) Triage & scope:
  - Confirm which tenant(s) are affected: check alert labels and metrics.
  - Query control-plane health API: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://controlplane.redwood.internal/v1/tenants/<tenant>/status
  - Check agent heartbeat resync rate and last successful registration timestamps (Grafana dashboard: SRE > Private Controlplane > Tenant Heartbeats).
- 2) Rapid network sanity checks:
  - From a jump host in the same region, run: sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -i eth0 "udp and host <agent_ip>" and capture 60s to inspect ICMP and source port behavior.
  - Run traceroute for UDP and TCP: sudo traceroute -U -p 123 <control-plane-ip> and sudo traceroute -T -p 443 <control-plane-ip> to compare path differences.
  - Check control-plane host kernel counters for UDP errors: sudo cat /proc/net/snmp | grep Udp
- 3) Customer comms template (fast):
  - "We are seeing UDP error counts and packet drops between your agents and our control plane that started shortly after your firewall change at <time>. Can you confirm whether stateful UDP inspection or per-flow limits were enabled? If possible, temporarily allow UDP ports <list> or roll back the most recent ACL change while we investigate."
- 4) Short mitigation knobs:
  - If customer agrees, ask them to: 1) revert change; 2) add specific allow rules for agent IP ranges and control ports; 3) disable UDP stateful inspection for agent flows.
  - Internally: increase heartbeat backoff via feature flag: Admin UI > Private Configs > control.heartbeat.backoff_ms = 5000 (note: this is a temporary band-aid; do not leave enabled long-term).
- 5) Escalation:
  - If customer cannot rollback or network appliance is managed by a third party, open a runbook escalation to Solutions Eng and Account team and consider scheduling a joint troubleshooting session with packet captures and appliance vendor support.

Checklist items to add to onboarding and runbooks (quick list):
- Explicit firewall template with TCP and UDP port list and example ASA/iptables rules.
- Note about stateful UDP inspection: recommend disabled or disabled for agent IP CIDRs.
- Test commands for customers to run before cutover: tcpdump + traceroute + simple UDP echo test (socat - UDP).
- Alerting: add per-tenant UDP error and ICMP unreachable fast alerts.
- Synthetic checks: periodic control-plane -> tenant UDP/TCP probe.

Open questions / items for design discussion:
- What is the minimal set of control messages that must always have reliable delivery? Can we gate those behind TCP only?
- How much telemetry overhead is acceptable to add per-tenant to detect network appliance interference early?
- Should we bundle a light-weight UDP-friendly agent helper that negotiates a TCP fallback automatically?

Appendix: useful commands and traces captured during incident (redacted):
- tcpdump excerpt: "20:27:12.123456 IP 10.0.5.27.45678 > 34.120.8.11.123: UDP, length 48" followed by a burst of "ICMP 34.120.8.11 udp port 123 unreachable
" repeated.
- Kernel counters: Udp:InDatagrams 123456 InErrors 432 OutDatagrams 120987
- Quick grep to see ICMP in system logs: sudo journalctl -u network-agent | grep -i icmp | tail -n 50

Related tickets and notes:
- INFRA-3421: "tenant-382 intermittent agent registration failures" (primary incident ticket).
- SRE-1184: "add UDP error counters and fast alerting" (follow-up engineering task).
- Slack thread: #sre-oncall, message id: message12345 (contains customer provided firewall change log).

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- For customers who are very conservative on firewall policies, our onboarding should include a short interactive checklist and a small set of unit tests they can run pre-cutover. Could be shipped as a CLI helper.
- Consider a hardened control-plane port that uses TCP or TLS-only for registration and then switches to UDP for lower-latency ops where safe.

Next steps (immediate):
- Jamal to add alert and send PR for dashboard panels.
- Irene to update Private onboarding checklist and send to Solutions Eng for review.
- Marcus to spike TCP fallback prototype and create design doc.
- Samantha to update confluence runbook and mark this doc as final after owners confirm ETA items.
